The mechanism

Choose a module basis that exposes composition

A divisibility condition in two variables can conceal a one-variable composition. The proof expands in a suitable free-module basis and compares the surviving coefficients along the diagonal. The new working coordinates isolate the restriction imposed by divisibility.

What becomes elementary: A polynomial divisibility question becomes a controlled remainder and coefficient calculation.

Read the free-module proof and work through the extraction example. The Galois and Frobenius companion in the Tensorgami archive supplies a second route with its own hypotheses; compare which work each representation makes immediate.

Explore further constructions. Edition dates, sources and reference chapters identify the scope of each study.

1 · Statement and first comments

Separated polynomials, namely polynomials of the form , occur naturally in factorization problems, fiber products of polynomial maps, and functional equations with conjugate branches. Remark 9.2. The word “irreducible” is not needed in the argument. The quadratic branch polynomial may or may not be irreducible over , depending on the field. What matters is that the three branches are distinct over an algebraic closure of . The main divisibility criterion itself does not require any separability hypothesis; separability only enters here because we infer divisibility from vanishing at distinct branches.

12 · Some uses of the criterion

The theorem is a useful algebraic test for recognizing common composition hidden inside a divisibility relation.

  1. Composition detection. If , then lies in the subring , lies in the subring , and the two factorizations use the same outer polynomial .

  2. Fiber products of polynomial maps. The quotient-ring identity

    says that the only functions on the fiber product which separately come from the two factors are those descending from the base.

  3. Separated-variable factorization. Problems involving divisibility or factorization of polynomials of the form often reduce to understanding which one-variable polynomials are composite with a prescribed inner polynomial. The residue-rectangle method provides a direct coefficient comparison without needing irreducibility of .

  4. Functional equations with conjugate branches. Proposition 10.1 gives an exact criterion over every field: constancy on the generic fiber, with its multiplicities retained, is equivalent to . The multiplicities are measured by Hasse derivatives. Constancy on geometric points alone is equivalent to , where is the generic fiber’s inseparable multiplicity. The cubic functional equation in Proposition 9.1 is the case .

  5. Characteristic-free arguments. The proof of Theorem 1.1 uses only polynomial identities, freeness over subrings generated by nonconstant polynomials, and the diagonal specialization . It therefore works over arbitrary fields, including fields of positive characteristic.

13 · Summary of the mechanism

The proof has four moving parts.

  1. The one-variable decomposition

    records every polynomial uniquely by its residue degree modulo .

  2. The two-variable decomposition

    gives a residue rectangle.

  3. In that rectangle, the identity

    becomes the coefficient system
    Setting kills the factor , forcing all off-origin coefficients of and to vanish and forcing the origin coefficients to agree.

  4. Once the common composition is known, the outer polynomial is extracted by dividing by . The -constant remainder is exactly the desired outer polynomial.

Thus the divisibility condition is exactly equivalent to the existence of a common outer polynomial with
